Amazon Celebrates 15 Years in Eastern Oregon with Community Day
The event brought families, community leaders, and Amazon employees together for a day filled with hands-on STEM activities, live demonstrations, giveaways, and free food. Local partners helped make the day special, with Eastern Oregon University's GO STEM program and Sage on the Go leading interactive science and engineering activities, including a data center learning game designed just for kids. The South Morrow Art Center set up creative stations for all ages, and Creativo District offered free haircuts to help boost confidence in local youth.
A parent and child engage with one of the creative stations at Amazon's Community Day.
One of the day's highlights: five lucky attendees were selected in a drawing to each direct a $2,000 donation to a local nonprofit of their choice serving Morrow and Umatilla Counties.
"Amazon's presence in Eastern Oregon for the past 15 years is only possible because of the families, local organizations, and community leaders, and we don't take that partnership for granted," said David Tanner, director of infrastructure operations for Amazon Web Services. "We look forward to continuing to grow together and finding new ways to give back to the community we're proud to call home."
Amazon has operated in Eastern Oregon for more than 15 years, with more than 2,500 employees working in Amazon's data centers across the region. The Community Day offered a chance for families to connect directly with Amazon's local team, explore hands-on STEM programming, and learn about resources available in their community.

How Amazon is protecting energy affordability in Indiana
Data centers
 house the computers that make the modern internet possible. As more Americans rely on data centers to power their daily lives, more energy is needed to run them.
In 
Indiana
, Amazon has data centers in two utility service areas: 
Northern Indiana Public Service Company
 (NIPSCO) in Northwestern Indiana and 
Indiana Michigan Power
 (I&M) in the Northeast and East Central regions. In both cases, we entered long-term agreements that ensure our energy costs are not passed on to our neighbors.
Indiana Michigan Power (I&M)
Amazon reached an agreement with I&M that provides binding, long-term financial commitments so that our costs are not passed on to existing customers.
Amazon covers 100% of the electricity costs for our data centers and guarantees I&M payment for at least 80% of our projected demand, whether we use that capacity or not. If Amazon uses less capacity than expected, we absorb the cost—not ratepayers.
Amazon is also funding $2.5 million in energy assistance and efficiency programs for low-income I&M customers through the Indiana Community Action Association, helping lower bills for families struggling to make ends meet.
I&M announced a 3.6% reduction
 in residential utility bills in May, followed by an 
additional 5% reduction in August
—driven in part by revenue from large users like data centers.
Northern Indiana Public Service Company (NIPSCO)
Amazon and NIPSCO developed a first-of-its-kind framework to add up to 3 gigawatts of new capacity to the Indiana power grid without increasing costs for other ratepayers. Amazon pays fees to use existing power lines and to cover the costs of any system upgrades needed to power our data centers. The agreement is estimated to generate $1.25 billion in savings for NIPSCO customers over the next 15 years.
What this means for Hoosiers
At Amazon, we believe data center growth should strengthen the grid, help lower electricity costs, and make power more reliable. That's our commitment to the 
communities where we operate
.

Amazon employees pack 450 meal kits, make a home accessible in North Carolina
Forty-five Amazon employees volunteered nearly 170 hours across three projects during the United Way of Richmond County's annual Days of Caring.
Amazon employees smile on a newly rebuilt deck for a resident during the United Way of Richmond County's annual Days of Caring.
Amazon is building a new data center campus in Richmond County, North Carolina, but the team didn't wait for operations to begin to start getting involved. From September 16–18, 45 employees fanned out across the county for the United Way of Richmond County's annual Days of Caring, volunteering on three projects and logging nearly 170 hours combined.
Feeding kids on the weekends
The team spent the morning with Backpack Pals, assembling more than 450 weekend meal kits for children across Richmond County schools. The kits make sure students have something to eat when the cafeteria isn't an option. Many of our employees are parents, so this project was personal.
Making Ms. Vickie's home accessible again
Part of the team joined Habitat for Humanity of the NC Sandhills for a multiday volunteer effort to demolish and rebuild three decks for Ms. Vickie, a local resident who could no longer safely get in and out of her home. Our team was proud to be part of the crew that made her home accessible again.
Getting the food pantry ready
The rest of the team deep-cleaned and restocked Our Daily Bread Food Ministry's food pantry from floor to ceiling—organizing shelves, rotating inventory, and preparing it to serve the families who depend on it most.
What's ahead
This was the first volunteer day for the team, but it won't be the last. They're already planning more community projects before the end of the year.
"We know actions matter more than words. 70% of our team showed up on a single Friday to pack meal kits for kids, rebuild a deck, and restock a food pantry—and we're just getting started. We want to be the kind of neighbor who's there when it counts," said Kelly Felix, data center cluster operations leader for North Carolina.

How we're building responsibly in Wharton County, Texas
Amazon has been building and operating data centers for nearly two decades. In that time, we've proven that we are not only good neighbors, but committed long-term collaborators in the communities where we operate and our employees live. As this project in Wharton County progresses, we want to share what we are planning, how we intend to use water and power, and what the project will mean for people who live nearby.
What we're building
We are currently planning a data center campus outside of Boling, Texas, about 10 miles southeast of Wharton. The project will support at least 300 full-time positions, with 150 full-time roles by mid-2027, with wages well above the county average. The construction process will generate thousands of additional jobs and expanded opportunities for local contractors and small businesses.
We see long-term potential here and are evaluating options for future investment, but today only have plans for 13 buildings.
As with any project of this scale, development will occur in stages. Site preparation is already underway, and we are committed to providing transparency and updates to the community as the project progresses. Ultimately, each location is driven by campus size and may evolve over time.
Clear answers on water
The 13 buildings planned on the Wharton County campus will not use water for cooling. No groundwater will be used for data center cooling at this site. As we evaluate future investment or expansion at this campus, we are working directly with the regional and local water authority to develop responsible, nonpotable water solutions for any potential cooling needs. This is part of our standard process for finding the most efficient method for operating our data centers, with a key tenet of ensuring that our projects do not negatively impact water needs for the surrounding community.
Besides cooling, data centers use water for everyday needs like bathrooms, cleaning, and fire suppression systems. For our current plans, potable use is limited to approximately 16,000 gallons per day, equivalent to roughly 54 households or a typical office building with a similar number of employees.
Replenishing local water resources
Amazon is committed to being water-positive globally by 2030, meaning we'll return more water to communities than we use in our data center operations—and we're already 75% of the way there.
Amazon is actively working with local organizations to develop water-positive programs, including in Wharton County, that will return more water than we use to the local watershed.
As part of this project, Amazon is funding a water replenishment project in Wharton County that helps local farmers adopt Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD) irrigation practices—reducing flood-based irrigation demand by 25% or more without reducing crop yields—in the lower Colorado River watershed, where both area farmers and other users draw from the same surface water source. This effort is expected to replenish more than 225 million gallons of water per year over a 10-year period.
Powering our operations responsibly and supporting the Texas electric grid
Amazon works closely with energy providers in Texas to pay the full costs of powering our operations—so those costs are not passed to other customers. These investments often extend beyond our immediate needs and help modernize the broader grid.
We do not plan to build or operate a gas plant at our Wharton County site. We are actively working with energy companies to explore power supply options in ERCOT, delivered by existing transmission infrastructure and substations we are funding on-site. We remain committed to responsible energy procurement, having invested in more than 10 GW (gigawatts) of energy supply in Texas—enough to power roughly 8 million U.S. homes—and we continue pursuing both dispatchable and renewable solutions to meet our needs.
Backup generation and grid reliability
We rely on the utility grid to power our data centers. To ensure uninterrupted service for the critical customers who depend on our infrastructure—including hospitals, schools, and emergency services—our data centers include backup generators in case of rare power disruptions. These generators are an essential safety feature, not a primary power source, and they run very infrequently—mostly for brief mid-day tests to ensure they are ready and reliable when needed.
We take air quality seriously. Our backup generators use Tier 4 compliant emissions control technology—the most stringent EPA standard for diesel engines—which significantly reduces nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds, and particulate matter. These controls deliver the same environmental performance as Tier 4 certified engines, and we conduct comprehensive field testing as required by our environmental permits to verify they achieve the required emission reductions.
During grid emergencies, we actively participate in grid management protocols and will curtail our load or activate backup power—just like other large industrial users. We are also fully committed to complying with all Texas grid reliability standards, including Senate Bill 6.
Designing and building responsibly—our permitting and environmental review process
Building a data center campus of this scale requires extensive planning, design, and regulatory review—and we approach every phase with a commitment to doing it right.
Before any work began at the Wharton County site, we completed a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment, which found no contamination or recognized environmental conditions. The site has been agricultural pastureland and forestland since at least the 1940s. We also commissioned a thorough natural resources assessment by working with environmental consultants to evaluate the property's waterways, wetlands, and wildlife.
Our permitting and compliance work spans multiple areas:
Air quality: We work with state environmental agencies to secure and comply with all applicable air permits for our operations, including emissions from backup generators. We voluntarily invest in advanced emissions control technology that reduces pollutants well beyond minimum regulatory requirements.
Water and waterways: The campus layout achieves 100% avoidance of the jurisdictional stream—Gardner Slough—and its associated wetlands, with all buffer zones exceeding regulatory minimums. We are coordinating with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on the jurisdictional determination process for the property. We comply with all applicable water discharge permits and monitor water quality to meet or exceed regulatory standards.
Stormwater management: We build stormwater management infrastructure, such as retention ponds and drainage systems, to control runoff and protect local waterways and groundwater.
Wildlife and habitat: A qualified biological consultant completed a habitat assessment across the full property. No federally listed threatened or endangered species were observed on the development footprint. Migratory bird breeding areas were identified and flagged so construction crews knew where active or potential nesting habitat existed before any clearing began.
Building and site design: Throughout design and construction, we work with acoustic engineers to keep noise levels low and design our facilities to meet federal guidance for the health and welfare of surrounding communities. We implement noise mitigation measures including sound-dampening building materials, strategic placement of cooling equipment, visual screening, and acoustical enclosures for generators.
Spill prevention and emergency response: Every facility maintains a Spill Prevention, Control, and Countermeasure (SPCC) plan with regular training, monthly inspections, and established notification and cleanup protocols that meet all federal and state requirements.
We comply with all environmental regulations—including those related to water quality, air emissions, stormwater management, noise levels, and waste disposal—and work closely with environmental agencies throughout every phase of our projects to ensure we meet and often exceed all applicable standards.
Jobs, tax revenue, and community investment
This project will support at least 300 full-time positions—with 150 by mid-2027—at wages well above the county average. During construction and operations, the campus will employ plumbers, pipe fitters, electricians, project engineers, fiber technicians, line workers, and data center technicians. We're working with local organizations on workforce development programs to prepare residents for these roles.
We've established the Wharton County Community Fund with an initial $200,000 commitment for science, technology, engineering, and math (STEM) programming, youth recreation, veterans programs, housing, and other local priorities. We're also launching a dedicated project website with FAQs and a way for community members to share questions and feedback.
The project is expected to generate tens of millions of dollars in new tax revenue, providing sustainable funding for local schools, public safety, and infrastructure.
In summary, Amazon is committed to building responsibly in Wharton County—creating good jobs, generating sustainable tax revenue, and investing in the community while being thoughtful stewards of local water and energy resources.
We look forward to sharing updates as the project progresses.
FAQs
Will the data center be loud for nearby homes or businesses?
We work hard to ensure our data centers operate as quietly as possible in a way that respects our neighbors and the surrounding community. In addition to meeting all local noise regulations, we strive to design our facilities to federal guidance for the health and welfare of surrounding communities, which often are lower than the regulatory standards. We implement several noise mitigation measures including:
Sound-dampening building materials and insulation
Strategic placement of cooling equipment
Visual screening where needed
Generators that utilize acoustical enclosures and mufflers
Throughout design and construction, we work with acoustic engineers to keep noise levels low and ensure the facility fits comfortably within the surrounding community.
How is Amazon investing in Wharton County?
Amazon is committed to being a good neighbor throughout the construction process. We listen and engage with local officials and community members to address concerns proactively. We aim to minimize disruption while still being able to deliver meaningful benefits including new construction and long-term technology jobs, opportunities for local contractors and small businesses, and sustainable tax revenue that supports schools, public safety, and community services.
This project is expected to generate tens of millions of dollars in new tax revenue, providing sustainable funding for essential services, local schools, and infrastructure. We have also started the Wharton County Community Fund, with an initial commitment of $200,000 that will be used for STEM programming, youth recreation, veterans programs, housing, and other hyperlocal programs.
Will this impact the reliability of the grid?
We understand concerns about grid reliability, and we want to clarify how our data center operates within the electrical system. Our data centers connect to the high-voltage transmission system, not the local distribution lines that power homes and businesses in your neighborhood. Our facility uses the transmission system, which operates at much higher voltages and is completely separate from the infrastructure serving the community. Our power needs will not impact local voltage levels or increase the risk of brownouts in your area.
We are also fully committed to complying with all Texas grid reliability standards, including Senate Bill 6.
We actively participate in grid management protocols and will curtail our load or activate backup power during grid emergencies—just like other large industrial users.
Will this project impact my electricity rates?
Amazon works closely with energy providers in Texas to pay the full costs of powering our operations so those costs are not passed to other customers.
The electricity investments we make often extend beyond our immediate needs and help modernize the broader grid. We have invested in enough energy supply in Texas to power roughly 8 million U.S. homes, and we continue pursuing both dispatchable and renewable solutions to meet our needs.
In fact, a recent national analysis by the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and The Brattle Group found that states with growing electricity demand—including from sectors like manufacturing and data centers—saw lower retail electricity prices. Adding new customers spreads fixed grid costs across more users, which helps reduce pressure on rates.
How much water will this project use?
The 13 buildings planned on the Wharton County campus will not use water for cooling. No groundwater will be used for data center cooling at this site. Besides cooling, data centers use water for everyday needs like bathrooms, cleaning, and fire suppression systems. For our current plans, potable use is limited to approximately 16,000 gallons per day, equivalent to roughly 54 households or a typical office building with a similar number of employees.

This effort is expected to replenish more than 225 million gallons of water per year over a 10-year period.

Amazon is turning Spotsylvania's sewage water into a resource
When you flush a toilet, take a shower, or run a load of laundry, that water flows into the sewage system. In Spotsylvania County, it gets treated and discharged into the Rappahannock River. You may not think about it again.
Amazon and Spotsylvania County leaders celebrate the start of construction on a new water reuse system that will recycle treated wastewater to cool Amazon's data centers.
Amazon did. A new $480 million water project, built in partnership between Amazon and Spotsylvania County, will upgrade the Massaponax Wastewater Treatment Plant and add more than 20 miles of new pipeline to turn that wastewater into a resource. The system will produce the second-largest water reuse capacity in Virginia.
What this project does
The project conserves drinking water by directing reclaimed water to industrial customers. Preserving Spotsylvania's potable supply for residents and other business users.
How it benefits the community
Attendee signs a "purple pipe" to commemorate the project's launch. Purple pipes are used across the utilities industry to carry recycled wastewater, and this system will repurpose the county's treated wastewater to cool Amazon's data centers.
The county will own the system and can sell reclaimed water to other businesses, creating a new revenue stream. And residents won't see any of this on their water bills, because they aren't paying for it. Use of the system is also seasonal—typically late spring to early fall. During cooler months, the full capacity is available for other uses or can be returned to the river as it does today.
Amazon's commitment
Because of how we design our facilities, we cool servers with outside air about 96 percent of the year in Spotsylvania. Water enters the picture only during the hottest hours of the hottest days, roughly 4 percent of the time when outside air alone can't do the job. We use outside air because it balances water and energy usage. If we used traditional air conditioning instead, we would draw 25-35% more power from the grid.
We were the 
first data center operator
 in Virginia to cool with 
reclaimed water
. Globally, we are 
seven times more water-efficient
 than the average data center in the industry. 
As demand for cloud computing continues to grow, so does our commitment to doing more with less. In Spotsylvania, that means a county-owned system that turns waste into a resource, protects drinking water supplies, and creates lasting economic value for the community.

How we're protecting air quality in Richmond County, North Carolina
Amazon has invested more than $20 billion in North Carolina since 2010, including infrastructure and compensation to our employees, and in 2025 alone, donated $10 million to more than 25 local community organizations. In June 2025, we announced 
plans
 to 
invest $10 billion to build a new data center campus
 in Richmond County, creating at least 500 high-skilled jobs and supporting thousands more in construction and the supply chain. We also signed a multibillion-dollar agreement with Corning to produce optical fiber for data centers, creating 1,000 jobs at Corning’s manufacturing facilities across North Carolina and supporting hundreds of additional construction jobs—continuing our commitment to the state. Locally, we’ve partnered with the City of Hamlet Fire Department to provide $1.5 million to enhance public safety services in the region, provided $200,000 in community grants, and collaborated with Richmond Community College to provide workforce development programs that prepare local residents for skilled jobs in cloud computing and technology.
As we move forward with this project, we want to share how we're protecting the local environment. Amazon is committed to environmental responsibility in every phase of building and operating our data centers. We work closely with environmental agencies to ensure we meet or exceed all applicable standards.
Understanding Our Air Quality Permit
As part of this project, we've applied for an air quality permit from the North Carolina Division of Air Quality for the backup generators at our campus. Here's what that means and how we protect local air quality.
Why does the facility need so many generators?
Amazon data centers serve millions of customers, including hospitals, first responders, energy systems, and national security agencies. A single power failure could halt life-saving care, cut emergency communications, or cripple vital infrastructure. As a result, Amazon has built resilience into every layer of its operations, and backup power generators are critical to ensure our customers can access cloud computing during emergencies. Our Richmond County campus will include 21 buildings, and each needs backup generators to ensure reliability for customers.
How often will the generators actually run?
Backup generators run very infrequently — on average 10 hours per year — mostly for brief biweekly tests to ensure they are ready and reliable when needed during rare emergencies. All testing must meet local noise and permit requirements. This careful approach keeps facilities prepared for emergencies while minimizing any potential disruption to the community.
How much air pollution will the generators produce?
We take air quality very seriously. Our generators are carefully maintained and fully compliant with all Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality regulations. Beyond meeting these requirements, we install Tier 4 compliant emission control systems on our backup generators that significantly reduce emissions below required levels to protect public health. Our generators comply with the EPA's strictest standards for diesel engines.
Tier 4 is the cleanest EPA emission standard for diesel engine technology. Our data center facilities use Tier 4 compliant generators that achieve the same stringent emission reductions as Tier 4 certified engines:
90% reduction in nitrogen oxides (NOx)
80% reduction in carbon monoxide (CO)
40% reduction in volatile organic compounds (VOC)
70% reduction in particulate matter (PM)
To ensure our emission control systems meet Tier 4 standards, we conduct comprehensive field testing as required by our environmental permits. We routinely test a representative sample of our Tier 4 compliant generators at each facility to verify they achieve the required emission reductions.
How are emissions monitored and reported?
Throughout every phase of our projects, from initial planning through construction and ongoing operations, we work with environmental regulators to ensure that we comply with all environmental permits. These standards are enforced through multiple layers of oversight, including environmental permitting and compliance processes with local, state, and federal agencies, routine performance testing, ongoing monitoring and reporting requirements, and regular inspections. Amazon’s annual compliance reports will be publicly available via North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality and demonstrate that our facilities emit a fraction of the emissions that our permits limits allow.
In summary, this permit exists to protect local air quality. Generator operation will be limited to emergencies and required maintenance and testing. Our Richmond County campus will use Tier 4 compliant emissions controls, operate under strict state oversight, and report emissions data to regulators on a regular basis.

Amazon awards $500,000 to strengthen 46 local organizations in Northwest Louisiana
Forty-six organizations
 across Northwest Louisiana are turning local ideas into action with support from the Amazon Northwest Louisiana Community Fund, managed by nonprofit partner ChangeX. The fund awarded nearly $500,000 in grants of up to $10,000 to nonprofitst, schools, and individual community members across Caddo and Bossier Parishes and the greater Shreveport area. STACK Infrastructure, Amazon's data center development partner in the region, contributed $100,000 as part of a partnership to support community-led investment.
The grants were announced at a celebration on July 8 at Chef's Table by BeauxJax in Bossier City, Louisiana.
"We're proud to support the people and organizations doing meaningful work in Northwest Louisiana," said Afrika Alsup, community engagement manager at Amazon. "This fund puts resources directly into the hands of community members who understand what their neighbors need and are stepping up to deliver it."
"Supporting community-led projects like these is a meaningful way to invest in the people and neighborhoods around us,” said Kevin Hughes, chief external affairs officer at STACK Americas. "We're glad to help expand access to resources for organizations doing important work across the region."
From food rescue operations to youth robotics competitions to transitional housing for homeless families, the funded projects reflect the diverse priorities of the region, each one addressing a specific gap identified by people who know their communities firsthand.
Feeding families, students, and seniors
Grants will provide tens of thousands of pounds of food and weekend meal bags for children, secure infrastructure to rescue surplus restaurant meals and redirect them to people in need, expand home-delivered meals to seven days a week for homebound seniors, and deliver thousands of hot meals to families while their child is hospitalized.
Connecting young people to skills and opportunity

Understanding Our Water Infrastructure and Permit
As we progress our projects in Louisa, we're following the regulatory process, which involves applying for permits. Here's some context on our water discharge permit for the Lake Anna Technology campus and how we're working to be responsible stewards of local resources.
What is the permit for:
 We design our data centers for efficiency and build sustainability into everything we do. In Louisa County, we rely on outside natural air cooling for about 96% of the year and only use water-based cooling during the hottest periods, which is about 4% of annual operations. 
On only the hottest hours of the year, the facility uses a cooling system that evaporates water to safely cool air that in turn removes heat from the computers. As part of this process, cooling water needs to be periodically discharged; this cooling water is called ‘non-contact cooling water’. It never touches IT equipment, and it's treated before release in alignment with state environmental standards. This permit protects Lake Anna and local waterways while allowing us to discharge to Sedges Creek.
Where the water goes:
 The permit allows discharge to Sedges Creek, which flows into Lake Anna.
Will this heat up Lake Anna?
 No. On average, our daily discharge is approximately 0.0000882% of the volume of water in the Lake and will be discharged into Sedges Creek. The water will be at a cooler water temperature than

the warm side of Lake Anna where Sedges Creek eventually flows into. 
Why metals are listed in the permit:
 Very low concentrations of the metals listed in the permit are already naturally present in the water before being used by our data centers. As water evaporates during cooling, metal concentrations increase in the discharged non-contact cooling water—this is expected and is why monitoring will be required. The concentration of metals allowed in our discharge water is limited by the state and these requirements are determined by strict environmental and health standards. The limits for metals in our discharge permit are stricter than drinking water limits, meaning our discharge will be required to contain fewer metals than what is allowed in typical drinking water.
In summary, this permit exists to protect local water resources. Amazon’s system will minimize water use, treat water before discharge, avoid direct discharge into the lake, and operate under strict VDEQ oversight. Discharge would be intermittent, limited, treated, and monitored.
